title: U.S. House · Texas's 1st District
area: East Texas, including Tyler, Texarkana, Longview, and Marshall

context.text: Incumbent Nathaniel Moran (R) ran unopposed in the March 3, 2026 Republican primary. Yolanda Prince won a May 26, 2026 Democratic primary runoff against Dax Alexander, 72.3% to 27.7%.

candidates.name: Nathaniel Moran

summary.text: Nathaniel Moran is the Republican incumbent U.S. Representative for Texas's 1st Congressional District, an attorney who served on the Tyler City Council and as Smith County Judge before his election to Congress in 2022. He sits on the House Ways and Means Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the Ethics Committee, and is on the November 3, 2026 ballot after advancing from the March 3, 2026 Republican primary.

background.text: According to his official biography, he moved to rural East Texas with his parents shortly before his second birthday and grew up in Whitehouse, graduating from Whitehouse High School (Whitehouse I.S.D.) in 1993. (Ballotpedia lists Whitehouse as his birthplace.)
Attended the U.S. Military Academy at West Point for two years before transferring to Texas Tech University, where he earned a B.A. in Russian Language and Area Studies, an MBA and a law degree.

Moved to Tyler after law school and practiced civil law focused on business and commercial litigation and transactions; Ballotpedia lists him as an attorney and partner with the law firm Ramey & Flock, P.C.

Served on the Tyler City Council from 2005 to 2009. After being re-elected to a third term in 2009 and appointed Mayor Pro Tem, he resigned to move his family to Houston for three years so his oldest son could attend a school for the Deaf, then returned to Tyler and his law practice.

Served with nonprofit organizations including the Boy Scouts of America, the Discovery Science Place, Cancer Foundation for Life and the Tyler Area Chamber of Commerce, and helped start an education foundation for Whitehouse I.S.D.; he has also been a Sunday School teacher and church deacon.

Appointed Smith County Judge in 2016 to fill a vacancy and elected to a full four-year term in 2018, serving until his election to Congress in November 2022. The office is the presiding officer of the Commissioners Court and chief administrative officer of the county; he was appointed to the Texas Judicial Commission on Mental Health in 2021.
Won the 2022 election to succeed Rep. Louie Gohmert and took office January 3, 2023.
In the House, serves on the Ways and Means Committee (Oversight, Social Security, and Work and Welfare subcommittees), the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the Committee on Ethics.
According to his official biography, he and his wife, Kyna, have four children; his House website says the family lives in Whitehouse.

positions.summary: In a September 2024 official statement on voting for the SAVE Act, he said it helps secure elections by requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote.
positions.quote: The SAVE Act helps achieve these goals by requiring proof of citizenship when individuals register to vote and removing non-citizens from voter rolls.

record.text: Serves on the U.S. House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, among other committee assignments, in the 2025–2026 Congress.

candidates.researchNotes: Moran's official site lists issue pages (Economy, Education, Election Integrity, Pro-Life, Energy, Veterans, Border Security) but the content loads via JavaScript and was not accessible to extract specific position statements or quotes in this research pass.

candidates.name: Yolanda Prince
candidates.ballotNote: Won the May 26, 2026 Democratic primary runoff

summary.text: Yolanda Prince is the Democratic nominee for Texas's 1st Congressional District, a university project manager who won the May 26, 2026 Democratic primary runoff over Dax Alexander. Her BallotReady profile lists support for raising the minimum wage, teacher pay and a Medicare for All system.

background.text: Earned a bachelor's degree in public administration and public relations from Stephen F. Austin State University (1998) and a master's degree in public administration from the University of Texas at Arlington (2011), according to her BallotReady profile.
Has worked since 2022 as a project manager at Prairie View A&M University and since 2005 as CEO of Datwoman, Inc., according to her BallotReady profile.

Finished first in the March 3, 2026 four-candidate Democratic primary and advanced to a runoff with Dax Alexander. Local coverage said her campaign focused on education, civil and voting rights, and healthcare.
Won the May 26, 2026 Democratic runoff over Alexander, about 72 percent to 28 percent in reporting at the time, and became the party's nominee against Rep. Nathaniel Moran.

positions.summary: Campaign issues page says she supports raising the federal minimum wage to at least $15 per hour.
positions.quote: I support raising the minimum wage to at least $15 per hour so that full-time workers can earn a living wage and support their families without relying on government assistance.

positions.summary: Campaign issues page says she supports a Medicare for All single-payer system.
positions.quote: I support a Medicare for All single-payer healthcare systems, that guarantees health insurance coverage for every American.

positions.summary: Campaign issues page describes her as pro-choice and says she supports restoring Roe and protecting access to reproductive healthcare.
positions.quote: I am pro-choice. Decisions regarding reproductive healthcare belong to women, their families, and their healthcare providers—not politicians. I support restoring Roe and protecting access to reproductive healthcare.

positions.summary: Campaign issues page says she would advocate for ending the use of immigration detention centers.
positions.quote: I will also advocate for ending the use of detention centers.

candidates.researchNotes: Her campaign website (yolandaprince.com) was reviewed for her issue positions; no candidate questionnaire was found. No campaign website, candidate questionnaire, or public policy statements found for Prince. Her biography relies on Ballotpedia, a BallotReady profile and local news; her birthplace and pre-2005 career are not documented.
